name: Choctaw

allophone_rules.notes: Historic Byington/traditional spelling of the nasal vowels writes them as vowel+n/m before a further (different) consonant, e.g. pakanli -> [pakãːlih] (Broadwell 2006, A Choctaw Reference Grammar; no specific page located for this spelling convention). Nasal vowels are treated here as intrinsically long, matching the pattern this spec's gold benchmark shows for the modern macron-below convention (a̱ i̱ o̱), hence surface aː -> ãː rather than plain ã; this length claim rests on that distributional pattern, not on a page cite. Excluded when the nasal is itself geminated (hannali, yannash) or word-final (hakchin), where it stays a plain coda consonant.

The nasal that nasalises the preceding vowel (CHO_NASAL_*_PRECONSONANTAL) is itself absorbed and not pronounced, matching the traditional +C spelling convention (Broadwell 2006). Keyed on the following-consonant set so a geminate nn/nm (hannali) or a word-final n (hakchin) is left as a normal coda consonant.

notes: Choctaw (Chahta anumpa) — Muskogean language of Oklahoma and Mississippi, written in the Latin script, with three vowel qualities /i o a/, each contrasting short/long and oral/nasal (Broadwell 2006, A Choctaw Reference Grammar). Nasal vowels are treated as intrinsically long here; that is a distributional claim from this spec's gold benchmark, not something located at a specific page of Broadwell. This spec's gold benchmark mixes at least two written conventions rather than one: the modern Mississippi/Choctaw-Nation practice, which marks a nasal vowel directly with a combining macron below the vowel letter (a̱ i̱ o̱, mapped here to ãː ĩː õː), and the older Byington/traditional missionary spelling, which instead writes the historical vowel+n/m sequence before a further consonant (pakanli, pinti, imponna) and leaves the nasal vowel itself unmarked; CHO_NASAL_*_PRECONSONANTAL/_ABSORBED implement that second, more frequent convention as an allophone rule rather than a grapheme, since it is conditioned on what follows rather than being a fixed spelling. Long vowels are written doubled (aa ii oo) or, in the traditional convention, with an acute/macron. ⟨lh⟩ is the voiceless lateral fricative /ɬ/, ⟨ch⟩ = /tʃ/, ⟨sh⟩ = /ʃ/. ⟨e⟩ and ⟨u⟩ belong to the older Byington/missionary spelling still met in print; ⟨v⟩ and ⟨ʋ⟩ (the IPA-hook-v glyph used interchangeably with plain v in traditional-orthography sources) both write /ə/ (Broadwell 2006:16-18). Glottal stop is phonemic but not consistently written, and its presence is not predictable from the spelling of this gold set — many minimal orthographic doubles differ only in a word-final [ʔ] or [h] that is absent from the written form, which this spec cannot recover.
